title: Skin Biopsy: Choose the Technique That Preserves the Diagnosis
bottomLine: A biopsy is a diagnostic procedure, not merely tissue removal. Choose punch, shave/saucerization or excisional technique from the suspected disease, required depth, lesion size/site and downstream pathology needs; when melanoma or autoimmune blistering disease is possible, biopsy planning can determine whether staging or immunofluorescence remains interpretable.
recognize: Inflammatory dermatoses often need an active representative lesion; blistering disease may need separate lesional histology and perilesional direct-immunofluorescence tissue.
Suspicious melanoma requires a specimen that permits accurate depth assessment whenever feasible.
differentiate: A superficial shave may be appropriate for selected epidermal lesions but is not interchangeable with a depth-preserving biopsy for a lesion whose invasion depth changes management.
Destructive therapy gives no pathology specimen and should not substitute for biopsy when diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is plausible.
assessment: Define the clinical differential before choosing technique; review anticoagulants/bleeding history, allergy, site anatomy, infection, wound-healing risk and cosmetic/functional considerations.
workup: Photograph/measure/document the lesion and submit adequate clinical history plus site and differential to pathology; request direct immunofluorescence or special studies only when the specimen/site is appropriate.
management: Use sterile technique, adequate local anesthesia, hemostasis and wound care; place sutures when required and arrange removal/follow-up by site.
The clinician who orders the biopsy owns pathology review and definitive referral/treatment.
medicationSafety: Do not stop antithrombotic therapy reflexively for a minor skin biopsy; balance procedure bleeding risk against thrombosis risk and local protocol.
Check local-anesthetic maximum dose and epinephrine/site considerations rather than using one universal amount.
redFlags: Nondiagnostic biopsy despite persistent high clinical suspicion
counselling: Explain why the biopsy type and location matter and when/how results will be communicated.
followUp: Close the pathology loop, document concordance with the clinical impression and re-biopsy/refer when pathology does not explain a concerning lesion.
examTrap: Destroying or superficially sampling a lesion whose histologic depth is needed for diagnosis/staging.
oneLinePearl: Before touching the lesion, know what pathology question the biopsy must answer.

title: Cryotherapy and Electrosurgery: Treat Only What You Have Diagnosed
bottomLine: Destructive procedures are appropriate only when the diagnosis is sufficiently secure and histology is not required. Select cryotherapy or electrosurgery from lesion type, depth, site, skin tone, scar/pigment risk and patient preference; a suspicious melanoma or invasive SCC belongs to biopsy, not destruction.
recognize: Cryotherapy is commonly used for actinic keratoses, selected warts and some benign lesions; curettage/electrodesiccation is used for selected superficial lesions/tumours in appropriate sites.
differentiate: Pigmented/evolving lesions, indurated/ulcerated keratotic lesions and diagnostically uncertain lesions should not be destroyed before tissue diagnosis.
assessment: Confirm lesion identity, number/site/depth, healing tendency, circulation, neuropathy, immunosuppression, keloid history and cosmetic/pigment concerns.
workup: Biopsy first when malignancy, atypical infection or an uncertain inflammatory diagnosis remains plausible.
management: Use lesion-appropriate technique and local protocol; document treated site/diagnosis and provide wound-care instructions.
Plan repeat treatment or alternate therapy only after reassessment rather than automatically repeating destruction of a nonhealing lesion.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary topical antibiotics after uncomplicated clean procedures; petrolatum/simple wound care is often adequate.
Local anesthetic and electrosurgery safety follow product/device and patient-specific precautions.
redFlags: Nonhealing/bleeding lesion after presumed benign treatment
counselling: Discuss expected blister/crust, healing time and hypo/hyperpigmentation risk, especially in darker skin tones.
followUp: Reassess lesions that persist or recur unexpectedly and switch to biopsy when the diagnosis becomes uncertain.
examTrap: Repeatedly freezing a changing pigmented or indurated lesion instead of obtaining histology.
oneLinePearl: No histology comes back from a destroyed lesion—diagnose before you destroy.

title: Wound Care: Treat the Cause, Perfusion, Pressure, Moisture, and Infection
bottomLine: A chronic wound will not heal from dressings alone. Identify etiology and perfusion, remove pressure/trauma, manage edema and moisture, optimize nutrition/metabolic factors, debride when appropriate and treat true infection—not colonization—while escalating ischemia, deep infection or rapidly progressive tissue loss.
recognize: Venous wounds commonly occur in the gaiter area with edema; arterial wounds are often painful/distal with poor pulses; neuropathic pressure ulcers occur over load-bearing areas with sensory loss.
differentiate: Colonization/bioburden is not the same as invasive infection; inflammatory/vasculitic and malignant ulcers can mimic routine wounds.
assessment: Document size/depth, tissue, drainage/odour, surrounding skin, pain, pulses/perfusion, edema, pressure/footwear, sensation, glucose/nutrition, smoking and functional/social barriers.
workup: Assess arterial supply before compression when PAD is possible; culture deep/appropriate tissue only when clinical infection will change treatment, and image when osteomyelitis/deep abscess is suspected.
management: Use moist wound-healing principles with cause-specific offloading/compression/revascularization/debridement and appropriate dressings.
Treat cellulitis/deep infection systemically when present; source control and vascular/surgical/wound-specialty referral are essential when necrosis, abscess, ischemia or osteomyelitis is present.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine systemic antibiotics for a colonized chronic wound without clinical infection.
Avoid strong compression until clinically significant arterial insufficiency has been assessed/excluded according to the local vascular pathway.
redFlags: Nonhealing atypical ulcer with malignancy/vasculitis concern
counselling: Teach pressure relief/offloading, edema management, nutrition/smoking support and specific return signs rather than focusing only on dressing changes.
followUp: Measure healing trajectory; a wound that does not improve as expected requires cause reassessment rather than endless dressing rotation.
examTrap: Changing dressings repeatedly while ignoring ischemia, pressure or untreated edema.
oneLinePearl: The best wound dressing cannot overcome untreated cause or inadequate perfusion.

title: Leg Ulcers: Venous, Arterial, Neuropathic, or Atypical?
bottomLine: Leg-ulcer treatment depends on cause. Confirm venous versus arterial versus neuropathic/pressure versus inflammatory/malignant patterns, assess perfusion before compression, and escalate critical ischemia or deep infection; bilateral edema/erythema is not automatically cellulitis.
recognize: Venous ulcers often coexist with edema, hemosiderin/stasis changes and gaiter-area wounds; arterial ulcers often have reduced pulses, distal location, cool skin and ischemic pain.
differentiate: Neuropathic ulcers occur at pressure points with sensory loss; pyoderma gangrenosum/vasculitis/cancer can produce painful atypical nonhealing ulcers.
assessment: Assess pulses, capillary refill/temperature, edema, pain pattern, neuropathy, wound morphology/site, infection, mobility, diabetes/smoking and prior DVT/vascular disease.
workup: Use ABI/toe-pressure/vascular assessment when arterial disease is possible and interpret carefully in calcified vessels; culture only suspected infection and biopsy atypical/nonhealing ulcers when another diagnosis is plausible.
management: Venous disease generally needs compression once arterial safety is established plus edema/mobility care; arterial ulcers require vascular evaluation/revascularization consideration; neuropathic ulcers require offloading.
medicationSafety: Do not apply high compression blindly to a patient with possible severe arterial insufficiency.
Do not prescribe antibiotics for venous stasis inflammation without a convincing infection syndrome.
redFlags: Atypical painful undermined or malignant-appearing ulcer
counselling: Explain why circulation and pressure/edema control determine healing more than a particular dressing brand.
followUp: Track objective wound-area reduction and escalate nonhealing ulcers for vascular/wound/dermatology assessment.
examTrap: Starting compression from appearance alone without checking arterial perfusion in a patient with weak pulses.
oneLinePearl: Leg-ulcer treatment starts with vascular diagnosis, not the dressing cart.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada venous leg ulcer/best-practice resources

title: Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Chronic Follicular Inflammation, Not Poor Hygiene
bottomLine: HS is chronic recurrent follicular inflammatory disease with painful nodules, abscesses, tunnels and scarring in intertriginous sites. Diagnose from typical lesions/location/recurrence, stage burden and comorbidities, and use longitudinal medical/procedural therapy rather than repeatedly treating each flare as a hygiene-related bacterial abscess.
recognize: Recurrent nodules/abscesses, double comedones, draining sinus tracts and scars in axillae, groin, inframammary/perineal/buttock sites support HS.
differentiate: Simple recurrent furunculosis, infected epidermal cysts, Crohn-related perineal disease and pilonidal disease can mimic parts of HS.
assessment: Assess lesion/tunnel burden, drainage/pain, scarring, smoking, friction, metabolic/IBD/arthritis comorbidity, depression/anxiety and treatment access.
workup: Diagnosis is clinical; culture is reserved for superinfection/atypical infection questions rather than proving HS itself.
management: Use gentle local care/friction reduction plus anti-inflammatory antibiotic, hormonal/metabolic, biologic or surgical/deroofing approaches according to disease severity and current dermatology guidance.
Incision/drainage may relieve an acutely fluctuant lesion but does not provide durable control of chronic tunnels; dermatology referral is appropriate for recurrent/scarring/moderate-severe disease.
medicationSafety: HS antibiotics are often used for anti-inflammatory effect and should still have defined duration/monitoring rather than indefinite unreviewed use.
Biologic therapy requires infection screening and current product-specific monitoring.
redFlags: Longstanding atypical ulcerative lesion with SCC concern
counselling: Explicitly state HS is not contagious and not caused by poor hygiene; discuss smoking/weight/friction without blame.
followUp: Track new inflammatory lesions, tunnels/scars, pain/function and treatment adverse effects.
examTrap: Treating every recurrent axillary HS flare with incision and drainage alone and never offering disease-modifying care.
oneLinePearl: HS needs chronic inflammation control; draining one boil does not treat the disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association hidradenitis suppurativa resources

title: Hair Loss: Scarring or Nonscarring Changes the Urgency
bottomLine: Hair-loss evaluation starts by determining scarring versus nonscarring and patterned versus diffuse/patchy loss. Scarring alopecia is time-sensitive because destroyed follicles do not regrow; nonscarring disease is managed by cause after medication, endocrine/nutritional, autoimmune, traction and shedding patterns are assessed.
recognize: Androgenetic alopecia is patterned; alopecia areata causes smooth patches; telogen effluvium follows physiologic stress and is diffuse; traction causes distribution-specific loss.
Loss of follicular openings, perifollicular scale/inflammation or shiny scarred scalp suggests cicatricial alopecia.
differentiate: Tinea capitis can produce scale/broken hairs and inflammatory kerion; trichotillomania creates hairs of variable length; frontal fibrosing/lichen planopilaris are scarring disorders.
assessment: Assess tempo/pattern, scalp symptoms, hair practices/traction, pregnancy/postpartum/illness/weight loss, thyroid/iron risk, medications, androgen symptoms and autoimmune history.
workup: Target CBC/ferritin/thyroid or androgen testing to the clinical pattern rather than ordering a universal alopecia panel; fungal testing is used when tinea is plausible and biopsy is important for suspected scarring alopecia.
management: Treat the cause and use diagnosis-specific topical/oral/intralesional therapy; early dermatology referral is appropriate for scarring alopecia, severe alopecia areata or diagnostically uncertain inflammatory scalp disease.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy/reproductive plans affect minoxidil/antiandrogen and other systemic options; systemic immunomodulation requires disease- and drug-specific monitoring.
redFlags: Painful inflammatory scalp with rapid loss
counselling: Explain that shedding and permanent follicle destruction are different processes and set realistic regrowth timelines.
followUp: Use standardized photos/pattern assessment; escalate progression despite treatment.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with inflamed scarring alopecia that hair will regrow once the shedding stops.
oneLinePearl: The first hair-loss question is whether the follicle is still there.

title: Nail Disorders: Infection, Inflammation, Trauma, or Pigmented Warning Sign?
bottomLine: Nail dystrophy is not synonymous with fungus. Interpret the number/pattern of nails, skin/systemic findings and pigment morphology, confirm onychomycosis before systemic treatment, and urgently assess a new/evolving solitary longitudinal pigmented band or nail-unit mass for melanoma.
recognize: Onychomycosis can cause thickened brittle discoloured nails; psoriasis can cause pitting/onycholysis; trauma creates localized dystrophy; systemic disease can change multiple nails.
differentiate: Physiologic longitudinal melanonychia can involve several nails in darker skin, while a new changing solitary broad/irregular band or periungual pigment is more concerning for nail melanoma.
assessment: Assess duration, number of nails, pain/swelling, footwear/trauma, tinea pedis, psoriasis, medications, diabetes/PVD/immunosuppression and pigment change.
workup: Use KOH/culture/PCR or another validated mycologic test before systemic onychomycosis treatment; suspicious nail pigment/mass requires dermatology/nail-unit biopsy planning.
management: Treat confirmed infection according to extent/site/comorbidities; inflammatory nail disease follows the underlying diagnosis; drain/treat bacterial paronychia when indicated and correct mechanical trauma.
medicationSafety: Systemic antifungals have hepatic/drug-interaction risks and should not be prescribed from nail appearance alone.
redFlags: Acute painful paronychia with spreading infection
counselling: Explain that nail growth is slow and visual normalization may take months after successful treatment.
followUp: Reassess microbiologically confirmed fungal disease response and ensure suspicious pigment gets definitive dermatologic evaluation.
examTrap: Calling every dark longitudinal nail band on every skin tone fungus—or dismissing a changing solitary band as physiologic pigment.
oneLinePearl: Before months of antifungal therapy, prove fungus; before dismissing pigment, assess melanoma clues.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association nail fungus/nail health/subungual melanoma resources

title: Pediatric Dermatology: Age, Morphology, Toxicity, and Safeguarding
bottomLine: Common pediatric rashes are diagnosed from age, morphology, distribution and the child's systemic appearance. The NP must separate benign self-limited eruptions from meningococcemia/sepsis, eczema herpeticum, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki/MIS-C patterns, serious infection and safeguarding concerns—and use treatments appropriate to age/body surface.
recognize: Atopic dermatitis, diaper dermatitis, impetigo, viral exanthems, molluscum, warts and tinea are common; newborn and infant rashes have age-specific differentials.
differentiate: A well child with a blanching viral exanthem differs from a toxic child with nonblanching purpura; honey crust differs from HSV vesicles; diaper irritant dermatitis typically spares folds while candidal disease often involves them with satellite lesions.
assessment: Assess fever/toxicity, hydration, mucosal/eye involvement, blistering/purpura, itch/pain, medications/immunization, contacts/exposures, growth and whether lesion pattern/history raises non-accidental injury concern.
workup: Most common rashes are clinical; test/culture/biopsy only when morphology/systemic illness or treatment failure creates a specific question.
management: Use age-appropriate topical therapy, skin care and infection treatment; escalate toxic appearance, nonblanching rash, mucosal blistering, eczema herpeticum, extensive burns/skin loss or suspected abuse.
Dose systemic medications by current pediatric weight/age guidance and avoid adult-strength topical plans over large body surfaces without pediatric consideration.
medicationSafety: Young children absorb proportionally more topical medication over large body surface; choose potency/site/duration carefully.
Avoid aspirin in routine viral illness and avoid contraindicated age/pregnancy-family exposures according to current product guidance.
counselling: Teach caregivers expected course, safe skin care, medication amount/site and explicit return precautions.
followUp: Reassess persistent/atypical rashes, treatment failure, growth/sleep impact or recurrent infection; refer complex/scarring/genetic disease.
examTrap: Diagnosing a nonblanching purpuric rash in a febrile toxic child as a routine viral exanthem.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric skin disease, the child's systemic appearance outranks the rash name.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute-care dermatology/infectious disease principles
